extracted.intended_audience: literate general readership interested in manners, satire, and periodical essays (early 18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical/satirical essays about manners, character types, and literary taste—models and commentary useful for writing or judging Spectator-style witty moral essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of the 'Woman's Man'
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful 'Woman's Man' exhibits a particular persona: loose/negligent garb, soft and indolent manner, apparent effortlessness and unconcern, and a conversational style that imitates the women he courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and signs include: deliberate nonchalance; 'a pinched Hat, a measurable Step, and a sly surveying Eye' (strutting); having little officious attentions (knowing family news, what cures a cold, keeping spirits handy); being witty and humorous, inconstant yet pleasant; keeping women from comparing notes about him. Anti-pattern: a man of plain good sense (or a mere fool) will not succeed as well as one with these affected traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity and Whim as Social Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularities, whims, or peculiarities of behaviour that would make a man ridiculous among other men often recommend him to women; affectation and difference attract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that 'some Singularity in his Behaviour, some Whim ... that would have made him ridiculous among the Men, has recommended him to the other Sex.' Implication for performance/character: cultivated oddness can be a deliberate strategy to stand out; anti-pattern is being conventionally ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation and Social Proof Matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A man's reputation for being favoured by other women increases his appeal to an individual woman; jealousy and rivalry among women make a man more desirable if he is thought to have been successful elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactics noted include suggesting he is favoured by a rival to provoke jealousy, and that being 'loaded with the Favours of many others' is treated as a recommendation. Guidance: public signs of desirability (real or feigned) are valuable; secrecy or obvious exclusivity can reduce his allure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonchalance & Performance of Carelessness
rubrics_metrics.description: An appearance of unconcern and carelessness—an affected ease—is an essential performative quality for fashionable gallantry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an 'apparent Endeavour to appear unconcerned and careless.' The essay equates this with other performative arts (like hunting dress) and shows it as a deliberate social signal rather than genuine indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe Time and Place — Decorum in Behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Good breeding requires attention to the time and place of actions; behaviour must conform to the setting (e.g., decorum at church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letter-writers call for essays 'wholly writ upon good Breeding' and ask to 'dwell upon Behaviour at Church'—giving examples of giggling women during sermon as indecent. Suggested remediation: enforcement of decorum (e.g., a churchwarden holding up his wand). Practical rule: match comportment to situation to avoid impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider Natural Disposition (Indoles) in Education and Vocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Children's natural bent or inclination ('Indoles') should guide their education and the course of their lives rather than forcing every child into the same classical track.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes grammar-school masters who treat all children identically, producing 'hundred unaccountable Creatures ... whipped up into great Scholars' who never attain right understanding. Recommendation: examine a child's capacity early and, if suited, 'send to some Mechanics Way of Life' without regard to birth; cultivate natural talents rather than imposing uniform classical learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Corporal Punishment; Preserve the Child's Spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishing by blows or lashings is harmful to a child's moral and intellectual development; shame and honour are preferable corrective means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues corporal punishment 'brings [the child] below the Existence of a rational Creature' and 'extinguishes' virtue. Guidance: use shame/honor and appropriate discipline; do not 'whip on to their fourteenth or fifteenth Year' regardless of capacity. Anti-pattern: the 'inexorable Blockhead' master who punishes without discerning the child's ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Practical Tracking Based on Capacity, Not Birth
rubrics_metrics.description: Promptly place children unsuited to scholarly pursuits into practical trades, judged by capacity rather than social rank, to avoid long unnecessary suffering and debasement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recommendation: 'Let the Child's Capacity be forthwith examined and sent to some Mechanick Way of Life, without respect to his Birth.' This saves children from degrading punishment and wasted time.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Constitutes a Great Genius
rubrics_metrics.description: True great genius is mostly natural: prodigious, spontaneous powers that produce works admired without reliance on learned rules or artifice; often 'wild' and extravagant rather than scrupulously correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay distinguishes 'great natural Genius' (Homer, some ancients, Pindar) from 'Bel Esprit' refined by art and polite reading. A great genius 'by the meer Strength of natural Parts, and without any Assistance of Arts or Learning, have produced Works that were the Delight of their own Times.' Guidance: recognize that force and daring can outweigh nicety, and that genius cannot be manufactured simply by imitating those irregularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Mechanically Imitate 'Great' Irregularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to reproduce the irregularities of great natural geniuses by rule results in ridiculous, artificial imitations (e.g., Pindaricks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay criticizes those 'following Irregularities by Rule' and 'straining after the most unbounded Flights of Nature'—a lampoon of formulaic imitation. Practical guidance for writers: cultivate genuine force and feeling rather than contrived irregularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Force and Correctness — Value of 'Bienséance'
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern taste (especially in colder climates) prizes nicety, correctness, and decorum (bienséance), which can temper the raw force of ancient genius; good writing navigates between spirit and appropriate correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay notes that ancients often failed in 'decency of the Comparison' and that the rule of bienséance was discovered later. Implication: writers should balance elevated imagination with standards of propriety suitable to their audience and climate; excessive irregularity will invite ridicule from more nicety-minded readers.
